text: Exploratory data analysis is the work you do before you model, report, or build a dashboard: getting to know data well enough to ask good questions and avoid embarrassing mistakes. You already have the tools, pandas, statistics, matplotlib, seaborn. This chapter is about using them together in a repeatable order.

EDA isn't making every chart and seeing what looks interesting; that produces a pile of plots and no conclusions. Think like a detective: hold a question, look for evidence, let what you find sharpen the next question. Write questions down before you plot. Be suspicious of your data. And keep a running list of every surprise.

A workable five-stage order. Frame the question. First look: shape, types, missing values, duplicates. One variable at a time. Two or more variables together: relationships, group differences, correlations. Decide and record what to clean, keep, and investigate further. You will loop back, and that's normal.

This chapter uses one seeded, illustrative customer table, five hundred rows. I deliberately planted problems: twenty missing ages, and two enormous spend values hiding in the data. Real data always has some; EDA is how you find them.
The first look: shape is five hundred rows, seven columns. info shows age has only four hundred eighty non-null values, twenty missing; every other column is complete. Duplicated rows: zero.

Check the target you care about. churned value_counts shows seventy-nine point four percent stayed, twenty point six percent churned, an imbalance that matters later when you model. Then describe: total_spend has a mean of one eighty-eight point one but a median of only one twenty-four point four, and a maximum of ninety-eight hundred. Mean well above median plus a huge maximum is a signal to chase down.
EDA is a loop: question, look, notice, decide, repeat. Always start with shape, missing values, duplicates, and the balance of your target. Next: studying one variable at a time.
